Regular Council
Regular Council meetings are held on the second Wednesday of each month, with Closed Session starting at 5:30 p.m. when required, and Open Session starting at 6:30 p.m. Meetings are held as hybrid meetings to allow for in person and electronic participation. Residents may attend the meeting in person in Council Chambers at the Township's Municipal Centre or watch the live stream.
  Members of the Public wishing to submit Public Comments can do so in writing to the Clerk no later than 12:00 pm (noon) on the day of the meeting. Members of the Public may request their comments to be read by the Clerk or present their comments orally. Only Public Comments related to an item on the agenda listed under Reports, Correspondence and By-laws will be considered.

SECTION MENU
Agendas and Minutes are public documents. You may view Council agendas and meeting minutes online from 2006 to the present via the Township of Algonquin Highlands CivicWeb Portal.
To access Council agendas and meeting minutes prior to 2006, please contact the Clerk and the documents can be manually retrieved.

 Potential Municipal Equipment Operator Course
Recommended Motion:
BE IT RESOLVED THAT:
Whereas municipal public works departments from across the Province of Ontario provide invaluable services to our communities ensuring the health and safety of all residents;
And Whereas if it was not for our municipal public works employees from across the Province of Ontario maintaining our public roads systems, our communities would not be able to function as emergency personnel could not respond to calls, school buses could not get our children to school, residents would not be able to get to work, school or appointments and many more basic functions would not be able to happen;
And Whereas municipal public works departments are already feeling the impacts of a labour shortage, which will only be exasperated over the next three to five years, which will cause levels of service municipalities are able to provide to ensure the health and safety of our residents to decrease;
And Whereas there is currently no provincial-wide course that properly trains potential municipal public works employees, specifically relating to municipal heavy equipment.
Therefore It Be Resolved that the Township of Amaranth supports the work of the Association of Ontario Road Supervisors to develop a Municipal Equipment Operator Course to address this issue;
And That the Township of Amaranth calls on the Province of Ontario’s Ministry of Labour, Training, Immigration and Skilled Trades to fully fund the Municipal Equipment Operator Course in 2024 through the Skills Development Fund;
And That a copy of this resolution be sent to the Minister of Labour, Training, Immigration and Skilled Trades David Piccinni, the Township of Amaranth’s Member of Provincial Parliament Sylvia Jones and the Association of Ontario Road Supervisors.

Recommended Motion:
BE IT RESOLVED THAT:
Whereas current provincial-municipal fiscal arrangements are undermining Ontario’s economic prosperity and quality of life;
Whereas nearly a third of municipal spending in Ontario is for services in areas of provincial responsibility and expenditures are outpacing provincial contributions by nearly $4 billion a year;
Whereas municipal revenues, such as property taxes, do not grow with the economy or inflation;
Whereas unprecedented population and housing growth will require significant investments in municipal infrastructure;
Whereas municipalities are being asked to take on complex health and social challenges – like homelessness, supporting asylum seekers and addressing the mental health and addictions crises;
Whereas inflation, rising interest rates, and provincial policy decisions are sharply constraining municipal fiscal capacity;
Whereas property taxpayers – including people on fixed incomes and small businesses – can’t afford to subsidize income re-distribution programs for those most in need;
Whereas the province can, and should, invest more in the prosperity of communities;
Whereas municipalities and the provincial government have a strong history of collaboration;
Therefore, Be It Resolved That the Province of Ontario commit to undertaking with the Association of Municipalities of Ontario a comprehensive social and economic prosperity review to promote the stability and sustainability of municipal finances across Ontario;
And That a letter be sent to request advocacy in advance of the Provincial budget to the Premier, the Dufferin-Caledon MPP and local municipalities.

SECTION MENU
Members of the public who wish to make presentations to Council on their own behalf or on behalf of companies/organizations are called delegations.
Any member of the public wishing to appear before Council must adhere to the following guidelines, which are outlined in Amherstburg Council's Procedural By-law 2023-085:
9.1 The Town of Amherstburg actively encourages public engagement by inviting members of the community to participate in Council and Committee meetings, fostering a sense of inclusivity and transparency in local governance.

9.2 A delegation is a person intending to address the Council or Committee on a matter listed on the agenda where a decision of the Council may be required.

9.3 Delegations are permitted from the gallery during statutory public meetings under the Planning Act, or in accordance with any other legislation as required. Delegations are not required to give written notice to the Clerk but are encouraged to do so in order to facilitate the efficient conduct of the meeting.

a) Requests to participate electronically in a Public Hearing item are required to be submitted to the Town Clerk by noon on the last business day before the day of the meeting.

b) Delegation requests regarding any aspect of an official plan amendment, zoning by-law amendment or plans of subdivisions or condominiums will not be accepted between the conclusion of a public consultation meeting which was conducted in accordance with the Planning Act, and the final reading of the By-law.
9.4 Delegations during other proceedings of Council or Committees are permitted in relation to matters listed on the agenda stemming from all Administrative reports and by-laws; in accordance with the following:

a) Persons wishing to delegate at any Council or Committee meetings, shall advise the Clerk, no later than the Thursday before the meeting. Delegations shall provide their name, contact information, association with any organization (if applicable) and the agenda item to be addressed;

b) Delegation requests will first be reviewed to determine if it is merely seeking information, and if so, will be directed to the appropriate member of Administration for a response;

c) All delegations shall indicate the item on the agenda they wish to speak to, what action they wish the Assembly to take and shall provide a copy of any material intended for public distribution;

d) Delegations appearing before Council, who have previously appeared before Council on the same subject matter, shall be limited to providing only new information in any subsequent delegation request.

9.5 The Clerk may, from time to time, establish or amend procedures related to the Delegation Process, provided that such procedures do not conflict with the provisions of By-law 2023-085.

9.6 Unless otherwise authorized by resolution, or by a majority vote of the Council or Committee, a delegation shall be permitted to speak for a maximum of 5 minutes, excluding replies to questions from the members.

a) Only upon a verbal motion to extend the five-minute limit adopted by the majority shall the five-minute limit be extended and only one such extension is possible.

9.7 No more than 10 delegations will be heard per item of discussion by the Assembly.

9.8 Following each delegation, Members may ask questions of the delegate before receiving the delegation by way of motion.

9.9 Questions of staff by any delegate shall be received by the Chair and addressed when practical prior or during consideration of the subject item, after the conclusion and receipt of all delegations.

THE CORPORATION OF THE TOWN OF BANCROFT
BY-LAW NO. 83-2025
Being a By-Law to Establish a Schedule of Fees
for the Corporation of the Town of Bancroft
WHEREAS the Municipal Act, S.O. 2001, c. 25, s. 5 (3), provides that the powers of
every Council shall be exercised by by-law;
AND WHEREAS the Municipal Act, S.O. 2001, c. 25, s. 8 provides that the
Municipality, respecting a matter, may regulate or prohibit, require persons to do things
and provide for a system of licenses;
AND WHEREAS the Municipal Act, S.O. 2001, c. 25, s. 391 (1) authorizes a
Municipality to impose fees or charges on persons, for services or activities provided
or done by or on behalf of it;
AND WHEREAS the Planning Act. R.S.0. 1990. as amended, provides that Council
may prescribe a tariff of fees for the processing of applications made in respect of
planning matters;
AND WHEREAS the Building Code Act,1992, 5.0.1992, as amended, provides that
Council may require the payment of fees on applications for an issuance of building
permits and prescribing the amounts thereof;
AND WHEREAS the Council of the Corporation of the Town of Bancroft deems it
expedient to consolidate the fees and charges to be collected by the various
Departments;
NOW THEREFORE THE COUNCIL OF THE CORPORATION OF THE TOWN OF
BANCROFT HEREBY ENACTS AS FOLLOWS:
1. THAT the fees and charges for various municipal services are established as
shown in the Schedules attached hereto and forming part of this By-Law;
Schedule “A” – Administration
Schedule “B” – Animal Control
Schedule “C” – Building Department
Schedule “D” – Facilities
Schedule “E” – Fence Viewing
Schedule “F” – Finance Department
Schedule “G” – Licencing
Schedule “H” – Public Works Department
Schedule “I” – Planning
Schedule “J” – Signage Fees
Schedule “K” – Waste Management
2. THAT the fees established in this By-Law that are not subject to public
consultation, or which have not otherwise been amended prior to December
31st, shall be adjusted annually based on October Annual CPI calculations, as
per Statistics Canada, rounded up to the nearest dollar.
3. THAT the Municipal Treasurer shall add the fees and charges imposed
pursuant to this by-law to the tax roll for any real property in the Municipality
for which all of the property owners are responsible for paying fees and
charges under this by-law and collect them in the same manner as municipal
taxes in accordance with the Municipal Act, 2001 S.O., c. 25 s. 398.
4. THAT the fees and charges listed shall be subject to any applicable provincial
and federal taxes unless stated otherwise.
5. THAT where this By-Law establishes a fee or charge that also exists in
another By-Law that predates the effective date of this By-Law, the fee and
charge in this By-Law shall be the applicable fee and charge and the other By-
Law is effectively amended.
6. THAT this By-Law shall be referred to as the “Fees and Services By-Law”.
7. THAT By-Law 07-2025 is hereby repealed.
8. THAT the Mayor and Acting Clerk be and are hereby authorized to sign this
By-Law and affix the corporate seal thereto.
9. THAT this By-Law is enacted upon the third and final reading hereof.
Read a first, second and third time, and be finally passed, signed, sealed and
numbered By-Law 83-2025, on this 9th day of December, 2025.

Amendment to Noise By-law - Councillor Caputo
 WHEREAS excessive noise has the effect of interfering with the use and enjoyment of an individual’s property; and
WHEREAS the Municipal Act, 2001 authorizes municipalities to pass by laws regulating noise and other related nuisances in order to protect the health, safety, and well-being of persons, and the quiet enjoyment of property; and
WHEREAS residents are increasingly entertaining at home, including hosting backyard gatherings and outdoor social events, resulting in growing concerns regarding late-evening noise impacts on surrounding neighbourhoods; and
WHEREAS City events including live band concerts and sports events with loudspeakers, result in noise disturbance; and
WHEREAS the City seeks to balance reasonable residential enjoyment with the need to protect adjacent property owners from undue noise disturbances.
NOW THEREFORE BE IT RESOLVED THAT:
Staff BE DIRECTED to prepare an amendment to the Noise By-law to establish a maximum permitted noise level of less than 50 decibels after 11:00 p.m., applicable to all residential properties, including but not limited to noise generated from outdoor entertainment, backyard events, concerts, sporting events, amplified sound, musical instruments, or other sound-producing devices; and
Staff BE DIRECTED to conduct a review of noise by-laws and decibel limits in other Ontario municipalities, including but not limited to comparable urban and suburban cities, and report back on best practices, enforcement models, and recommended alignment opportunities; and
Staff BE DIRECTED to place the proposed Noise By-law amendment on a future Council agenda for consideration, accompanied by a report summarizing findings from the municipal comparator review and outlining any operational or enforcement implications.

Committee of the Whole
Menu
The City of Burlington's Committee of the Whole is a standing committee of Council.
The Committee of the Whole is responsible for considering all matters that do not properly fall under the jurisdiction of any other existing standing committees. The Committee of the Whole agendas are divided into the following sections:
Community and Corporate Services
Public Works
Growth Management
Meetings, agendas and minutes
The committee usually meets on Mondays at 9:30 a.m. and will continue Tuesday if required.
Check out our Council and Committees Calendar for meeting dates, agendas and minutes for upcoming and past meetings.
Committee members
All members of Council are members of the Committee of the Whole.  Each member of Council will serve as Chair on a rotating basis.

Refurbished Computer Request Form
The Municipality of Chatham-Kent periodically has used personal computing devices (desktops and laptops)
which can be refurbished and repurposed for local charities and non-profit organizations located in Chatham-
Kent. Although these computers are past the established life expectancy set by the Municipality, they may still
be of use to organizations. Please note the availability of computers varies throughout the year which may
cause delays in processing your request.
Interested organizations must accept the following terms listed below:
• Applications will be reviewed in the order which they are received.
• No guarantee is provided regarding types or quantities of equipment, or schedules.
• No guarantees are being made as to the age, completeness or operating condition of any computer.
• No software, operating system or installation key, support, disks or installation will be provided.
• Features of these machines will generally be those current five or more years ago.
• Recipients will need to do their own installation of their own operating systems and media.
• Recipients must agree that they are not acquiring the equipment for the purpose of selling it.
• Any optional hardware normally associated with a computer (such as a monitor, keyboard and mouse) must be
collected at the time of computer pick-up.
• Collection of equipment will occur at a time mutually agreed between the recipient and the Municipality of Chatham-
Kent during our normal business hours of operation. The Municipality will not provide any deliveries.
All machines are donated in “as is” condition – no guarantees, substitutions or support are possible.
Submit this form in one of three ways listed below:
 Complete this CK Municipal Computer Donation Request Form and hand it in to any Chatham-Kent Municipal
Centre service desk.
 OR complete the form, scan it and e-mail it to ckits@chatham-kent.ca.
 OR mail the completed form in an envelope addressed to: Manager, Service Management, Information Technology and
Transformation, Municipality of Chatham-Kent, 315 King Street West, PO Box 640, Chatham ON, N7M 5K8.

Priority: Deliver Excellent Service
We will deliver excellent service by creating a capable, sustainable, and efficient administration that is
connected to the community and our government partners.
1. Invest in staff.
a. Implement Comprehensive HR Strategy, including creating innovative workspace options &
advance flexible work policies.
2. Foster a culture of continuous improvement.
a. Develop a formal commitment to continuous improvement and innovation.
b. Develop a program management & evaluation framework.
c. Expand digital strategies.
d. Enhance customer service.
3. Improve communication and civic engagement.
a. Establish a corporate communications division.
b. Implement a Committee of the Whole to establish a framework to focus on strategic priorities
& community input.
4. Strategize intergovernmental advocacy.
a. Review the mandate of Council committees and develop a recruitment strategy.
b. Encourage Council delegates to attend provincial meetings.
c. Establish a framework and protocol for council members representing Chatham-Kent on
committees.
d. Build excellent relations with our Indigenous partners.
5. Maintain financial sustainability.
a. Optimize 4-year budgets and business planning.
b. Explore partnerships and shared-service opportunities.
c. Consider new revenue and financing sources.
Priority: Grow Our Community
We will grow our community with a focus on housing, infrastructure, services, workforce, and business
expansion we need to thrive.
1. Reduce barriers for affordability and attainability of housing supply.
a. Investigate additional options to incent all forms of “non-market: housing,” including student
housing.
b. Undertake feasibility / due diligence work on surplus municipally owned properties to ensure
“shovel readiness” for future senior level funding streams.
c. Work with non-profit housing providers to ensure affordable housing options.
d. Employ the “Housing First Strategy” by investigating opportunities of surplus government /
agency properties for housing as they become available.
e. Implement a “Yes in My Backyard” campaign to educate and garner support for a variety of
housing options.
2. Ensure an ample supply of available serviced land and strategic investments related to infrastructure
maintenance, renewal, and expansion.
a. Complete work on a new Official Plan and other key Master Plans to appropriately manage
growth and capital infrastructure investments.
b. Focus on immediate infrastructure investments that will leverage redevelopment,
intensification and underserviced designated land opportunities within urban growth areas
before expanding into underserviced greenfield (agricultural) lands.
c. Engage with utility providers to advocate and coordinate strategic investments to support
growth.
d. Explore the airport as an economic driver.
e. Develop opportunities for growth along the 401 corridor.
3. Strategic investments to diversify, rationalize assets and level of services.
a. Investigate ways to rationalize assets and level of service through the implementation of the
Asset Management Plan using a community wide approach.
b. Deliver the Fire Master Plan and develop an implementation plan.
4. Implement strategies to attract, retain and expand business and skilled workforce across all sectors.
a. Further develop enhanced concierge services for local businesses.
b. Enhance marketing strategies of the community as a place to make investments.
c. Support measures for talent attraction and retention, including immigrants.
d. Maintain / enhance quality of life aspects for an increasingly diverse population.
e. Work with community partners to increase education and training opportunities.
f. Establish an administrative Agricultural Advisory Committee with membership from various
agricultural organizations.
5. Plan and advance Downtown Renewal Projects.
a. Continue with the development of various downtown renewal projects and prioritize capital
investments.
4 | P age
Priority: Promote Community Safety & Well-Being
We will promote inclusion and the quality of life for “all ages and stages” in our community with investments
and programming in arts, heritage, recreation, social and health services.
1. Collaborate and invest in arts, culture, and heritage.
a. Develop Official Plan policies focused on the strategic integration of public art into appropriate
new developments.
b. Establish an Interdepartmental Public Art Team to accelerate municipal projects.
c. Update Cultural Master Plan.
d. Review and update Official Plan policies to define community goals and objectives related to
Built Heritage Preservation.
2. Provide supports for vulnerable community members & emergency preparedness.
a. Invest in strategies identified in the 3 pillars of the Community Safety and Well-Being Plan
(Community Awareness and Integration, Mental Health and Substance Use, Housing and
Homelessness).
i. People know where to get the services they need and when they need them.
ii. People can access local mental health and substance use supports and services.
iii. People have a safe place to call home.
3. Coordinate emergency and health services for delivery of community safety programming / services.
a. Invest in an Emergency Operations Center.
b. Work with the Province on short-term and long-term solutions regarding gas wells issues.
c. Fostering partnerships with other health service providers and explore shared services.
4. Develop policies to create an “all ages all abilities” community.
a. Engage community members when creating and developing policies.
b. Develop a Healthy Aging Strategy that addresses the full range of seniors’ services.
5. Advance Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Justice (DEIJ) & Truth and Reconciliation.
a. Invest in the DEIJ and Truth & Reconciliation programming / services prioritizing internal
milestones first.
b. Take the lead in a community wide DEIJ event.
6. Explore new and enhance existing recreational opportunities.
a. Undertake a new Parks and Recreation Master Plan that includes arena improvements and
community partnerships for recreational service delivery.
b. Expand and improve program and infrastructure delivery.
5 | P age
Priority: Ensure Environmental Sustainability
We will ensure the environmental sustainability of C-K by preserving the natural environment, reducing our
carbon footprint, and increasing the resilience of the community to climate change impacts.
1. Lead by example to reduce climate footprint & increase resiliency of Municipal operations.
a. Integrate a low carbon / climate resilient approach to the municipality’s asset management &
capital replacement program (i.e., upgrade at end of useful life).
b. Develop a corporate energy program focused on reducing operational costs.
c. Establish a revolving (self-replenishing) energy efficiency fund and energy management
information system to finance and monitor efficiency gains / cost savings realized by the
corporate energy program.
2. Enhance community resiliency to climate change impacts.
a. Complete a high-resolution heat island map to inform and prioritize heatwave resiliency
measures (i.e. urban tree planting).
b. Develop programs to help residents and businesses identify and address vulnerabilities to
heatwaves, flooding, and erosion.
c. Develop official plan policies, development standards and design standards focused on
increasing the resiliency of the built environment to the impacts of climate change (i.e.
naturalized stormwater facilities).
3. Promote community transition to a cleaner energy future.
a. Introduce a cost-neutral energy efficiency retrofit financing program for residents and
businesses.
4. Preserve natural heritage.
a. Champion voluntary stewardship (ALUS program).
b. Integrate urban trees into the Asset Management Program (start with inventory and condition
assessment).
c. Fund a permanent municipal street tree replacement and enhancement program.
d. Integrate natural heritage policies into Chatham-Kent’s official plan as per provincial
requirements.
e. Develop a municipal lands naturalization strategy to enhance nature and reduce operational
costs.
5. Improve sustainable mobility.
a. Integrate a Complete Streets design into all right of way projects.
b. Undertake a Sustainable Mobility Master Plan (cycling, transit, pedestrian accessibility,
roadway infrastructure).
c. Prioritize sustainable mobility investments to promote safety, accessibility for vulnerable users
and encourage alternative modes of travel.
d. Develop a municipal Electric Vehicle charger strategy.

Dear Municipal Clerk,
On behalf of the Bowmanville Health Centre (BHC), I am writing to request that the
Municipality of Clarington consider a deferral of the municipal development charges
applicable to our health facility expansion at 222 King Street East, Bowmanville. We
respectfully ask that this matter be placed before Council, and we welcome the
opportunity to speak to it at the appropriate hearing.
The Project
The BHC is constructing a new four-storey health facility on its existing campus to expand
access to community-based health care for the residents of Clarington and the broader
Durham Region. The building will consolidate and significantly expand essential services,
including:
• Expanded diagnostic imaging, including computed tomography (CT) services,
delivered by our imaging partner Durham Radiology
• A wound care program featuring hyperbaric oxygen therapy chambers, serving
OHIP-covered patients who currently travel outside the region for these treatments
• A purpose-built dementia care environment developed with the Alzheimer Society
• Expanded laboratory services, and
• specialty physician clinic space.
Every service in the building is oriented toward expanding community-based medical
services, reducing wait times, and keeping Durham residents' care close to home
Community Benefit and Diagnostic Volumes
The expanded imaging program is the centrepiece of this project's community value. In
partnership with BHC, Durham Radiology will operate an approved CT service expected to
Page 6
perform several thousand publicly funded scans annually for Durham’s residents who
today often have excessive wait times for this important imaging modality. Durham
Radiology is also actively pursuing the addition of magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
capacity, which would further reduce regional wait times and out-of-region referrals for
advanced diagnostics.
Bringing these services into a single community location directly advances the Province's
Your Health: A Plan for Connected and Convenient Care framework and the goals of the
newly designated Durham Region health team connected, convenient care delivered in the
community rather than in distant hospital settings. The Municipality of Clarington and the
Region of Durham have consistently identified improved local access to health services as
a regional priority, and this facility delivers precisely that.
The Request
The municipal development charges payable on this project total approximately
$367,781.81, due at the building permit stage — before construction is complete and well
before the facility can begin serving patients. Bowmanville Health Centre is a private health
facility, but the services the Health Centre delivers are publicly funded and community-
facing, including primary care, specialist care, and numerous medical services. We now
plan to add the CT program delivered by Durham Radiology, the wound care program,
expanded laboratory services, dementia care and other specialty services to serve
Clarington and Durham residents.
Like any health facility, these services generate no revenue until the building is open,
equipped, and operating, which is expected by Winter 2028. A development charge of this
magnitude, payable at the most capital-intensive stage of the project, places significant
pressure on the project's financial viability at precisely the point where every available
dollar is committed to construction and to bringing the approved CT service into operation.
A deferral of these charges until occupancy (anticipated Winter 2028) would materially
improve the project's ability to reach the point of opening its doors to the community, while

point at which the facility begins generating the activity that supports them.

the hearing. Thank you for considering this request in the spirit of partnership toward better
community health care in Durham Region.

SECTION MENU
Cobourg Municipal Council conducts its business through Standing Committee and Regular Council meetings.
Standing Committee Meetings
Standing Committees are affiliated with municipal divisions and overall priorities and policy decisions. Cobourg will now have three Standing Committees consisting of:
Community Services, Protection and Economic Development Standing Committee 
Meetings generally held on the first Wednesday of the month at 9:30 a.m.
Membership includes: Councillor Adam Bureau (Chair), Councillor Aaron Burchat, and Mayor Lucas Cleveland.
Public Works, Development Division Standing Committee
Meetings generally held on the first Wednesday of the month at 1 p.m.
Membership includes: Councillor Brian Darling (Chair), Councillor Miriam Mutton, and Mayor Lucas Cleveland.
Corporate, Finance, and Legislative Standing Committee 
Meetings generally held on the first Thursday of the month at 1 p.m.
Membership includes: Deputy Mayor Nicole Beatty (Chair), Councillor Randy Barber, and Mayor Lucas Cleveland.
Other Members of Council can attend standing committees of which they are not members to ask questions and hear information to prepare for Regular Council Meetings. Standing Committee members discuss items on the agenda and make a recommendation to Council for the action to be taken on the matter.
Regular Council Meetings
Following the Standing Committee meetings the recommendations of the Committees will be presented at a Regular Council meeting where a final decision will be made and published in the meeting minutes. See the calendar below for meeting information including dates and times, and to access Agendas, Minutes, and videos. Unless otherwise noted, meetings are open to the general public. 
Other Types of Council Meetings
The following meeting types are held by the Town of Cobourg Council:
Standing Committee
Regular Council
Public Council
Special Council
Emergency Council
Advisory Committees and Local Boards, and
Closed Council
The public may attend any of these meetings, except Closed Council meetings. Closed meetings are held in accordance with section 239 of the Municipal Act, 2001. 
See above for information on Standing Committee and Regular Council meetings.
Public Meetings
Public Council meetings are held to provide an opportunity for Council to receive comments from the public to assist Council in making a final decision. Public meetings are generally held on the third Wednesday of the month at 5 p.m.
Public meetings are held when changes to the following are being considered:
Certain by-laws (ie. Zoning By-law);
Licensing and Fees;
Master Plans (Parks, Waterfront, Parking, Transportation);
Official Plans; and
Other matters requiring public input.
Closed Meeting Investigator
Any person can request an investigation to see if Council has met in Closed Session for a valid, legal reason.
The Town of Cobourg has an Integrity Commissioner, Closed Meeting Investigator and Ombudsman. Fill in the Request Form for Closed Meeting Investigation and send it to the Legislative Services Department with the $25 fee.

Overview:
Executive Summary
This report provides Council with the annual Treasurer’s Statement respecting
development charge reserve funds for the year ended December 31, 2025.
The statement summarizes opening and closing balances, development charge
collections, interest earnings, and expenditures made from development charge reserve
funds during the fiscal year. It also includes the additional information prescribed by
Ontario Regulation 82/98.
During 2025, the Township collected $94,299.10 in development charges, earned
$6,998.46 in interest on development charge reserve funds, and applied $0.00 to
eligible growth-related capital expenditures. The total closing balance in development
charge reserve funds at December 31, 2025 was $279,168.86.
Background
The Township imposes development charges pursuant to the Development Charges Act,
1997 (the “Act”) and the Township’s applicable development charge by-law.
Development charges are collected to help finance the capital costs associated with the
increased need for municipal services arising from development. These funds are held
in separate reserve funds and may only be used for purposes permitted under the Act.
Subsection 43(2) of the Act requires the Treasurer to provide Council with an annual
financial statement relating to the Township’s development charge by-law and reserve
funds. Ontario Regulation 82/98 prescribes the content of the statement.
This report fulfills that annual reporting requirement for the year ended December 31,
2025.

Overview:
At the February 18, 2025, meeting, Council contemplated, debated and passed By-law
2025-09 - Being a By-law to Designate the Township of Douro-Dummer as a Site Plan
Control Area and Repeal By-law 2022-58. This new By-law is an update to the Site Plan
Control By-law that incorporated a series of housekeeping changes, and updates to
ensure the Township is complaint with provincial legislation. Most relevant to this
matter is section 5 of the By-law which states:
Notwithstanding the aforementioned exemptions, site plan control shall apply to the
following classes of development:
5.6. Any project that is within 120 metres of:
i) a wetland,
ii) an inland lake, or
iii) a river or stream valley that has depressional features associated with a river
or stream, whether or not it contains a watercourse unless a building permit was
issued on or before August 9, 2023.
This By-law effectively established a land-use planning policy in the Township that
directed staff to require a Site Plan agreement for development within 120 metres of a
wetland, lake or river / stream. The rezoning By-law attached to this report was
requested under this established policy.
At the December 2, 2025, meeting Council contemplated a report prepared by DM Wills
on behalf of the Township that responded to a request from late 2024 made by the
Environment Council for Clear, Stoney and White Lakes for a shoreline conservation By-
law in response to shoreline development concerns raised by Township residents. The
report identified that no By-law was necessary considering that the Township had
protections in place through a site plan control By-law.

Members of the public have the right to submit a complaint if they feel the Municipality held a closed meeting that did not follow the rules/exemptions listed in the Municipal Act, 2001, Section 239.2 (1).
The Closed Meeting Investigator's role is to conduct investigations upon receipt of a complaint in respect of meetings or part of meetings that are closed to the public to determine compliance with the Act or the Municipality's Procedural By-law and to report the results of such investigations to Council.
Our Municipality has appointed Ombudsman Ontario to investigate any complaints made to them by the public about closed meetings. 
Their duties include:
Conducting an investigation when they receive a complaint about a meeting or part of a meeting that is closed to the public
Determining whether the meeting complied with the Municipal Act and Municipal Procedural By-law
Reporting the results of the investigation

THE CORPORATION OF THE TOWN OF EAST GWILLIMBURY
BY-LAW NUMBER 2016-119
A By-law to provide for the Regulation of Construction, Maintenance and
Protection of Boulevards within the Town of East Gwillimbury
WHEREAS subsection 11{2)(6) of the Municipal Act, 2001, S 0. 2001, c. 25 as
amended ("the Act'') provides that a municipality may pass by-laws respecting the health,
safety and well-being of Persons;
WHEREAS subsection 11(2)(8) of the Act provides that a municipality may pass by-laws
respecting the protection of Persons and property;
WHEREAS subsection 30 of the Act provides that a highway is owned by the
municipality that has jurisdiction over it subject to any rights reserved by a Person who
dedicated the highway or any interest in the land held by any other Person;
WHEREAS subsection 27(1) of the Act grants a municipality the power to pass by-laws
in respect of highways over which it has jurisdiction;
WHEREAS subsection 28(2) of the Act grants a municipality jurisdiction over all road
allowances located in the municipality that were made by the Crown surveyors
[subsection 28(2)(a)) and all road allowances, highways, streets and lanes shown on
a registered plan of subdivision [subsection 28(2)(b)).
NOW THEREFORE the Corporation of the Town of East Gwillimbury enacts as follows:
1. DEFINITIONS:
1.1. In this by-law:
(a) "Back Lot Property" refers to that portion of a property where the rear yard is
adjacent to a Town or Regional road allowance;
(b) "Boulevard" means the portion of a Highway on either side of a Roadway;
(c) "Driveway Apron" includes that section of a driveway contained within the
municipal Boulevard;
(d) "General Manager" means the General Manager of Community Infrastructure
& Environmental Services or his or her designate;
(e) "Herbaceous Plant" means a plant without woody above-ground parts, with a
stem that dies back to the ground each year, but excludes turf grass;
(f) "Highway" includes the entire public road allowance;
(g) "Maintenance" means any action required to sustain a Boulevard including but
not limited to cutting, watering, removing debris or repairing damage to any
Driveway Apron or feature located within the Boulevard area;
(h) "Owner" means the lawful Owner of property, a lessee, tenant, mortgagee in
possession of property, or occupant of property;
(i) "Person(s)” includes an individual, association, firm, corporation, partnership,
sole proprietorship, trust, organization, trustee, and agent;
(j) "Region" means the Regional Municipality of York;
(k) "Roadway" means any portion of a Highway that is improved, designed, or
ordinarily used for vehicular traffic, and may include a curb and/or shoulder;
(l) "Sidewalk" shall mean that portion of the Highway that is intended for the use
of pedestrians and/or cyclists and which surface is finished with concrete,
asphalt or granular;
(m) "Town" means the Corporation of the Town of East Gwillimbury;
(n) “Tree” means any tree, shrub, hedgerow growing within the boulevard;
(o) "Traffic Control Device" means a sign, lane, meter, marking, space, barrier
or device painted or erected to guide, regulate, warn, direct restrict, control or
prohibit traffic;
(p) "Turf grass" means a perennial strand of plant that can form turf and withstand
mowing, traffic and/or wear;
(q) "Utilities" includes infrastructures such as cables, pipelines or structures that
are owned and maintained by the Town, Region, or other utility companies.
2. PLANTING IN BOULEVARDS
2.1 No Person shall plant or permit to be planted a Herbaceous Plant on a
Boulevard or section of Boulevard abutting his or her property that:
(a) exceed a height of 45 centimeters;
(b) impair drainage; or
(c) contain vegetables or grains;
(d) interferes with pruning, removal or replacement of Town Trees
(e) is within a distance of 3m or less from the base/trunk of a Town Tree
2.2. No Person shall plant or permit to be planted a tree on a Boulevard or section
of Boulevard abutting his or her property without written permission from the
General Manager.
2.3. Subsection 2.2. does not apply to Town planted Trees.
3. BOULEVARD MAINTENANCE OBLIGATIONS
3.1. Subject to any permission granted by the Town or Region, on a Boulevard
abutting his or her property, no Owner shall permit anything on the Boulevard
that:
(a) is protruding, sharp, dangerous in any way, or which may otherwise cause
damage/injury a Person or thing;
(b) restricts sight lines of pedestrians, cyclists or drivers of vehicles to
intersections, driveways, Sidewalks, walkways, travel lanes, or Traffic Control
Devices;
(c) inhibits or obstructs snow removal operations;
(d) obscures or obstructs access to fire hydrants, post office boxes, or other
installations belonging to the Town, Region, or any utility provider;
(e) is located within 0.6 metres of the Sidewalk, unless it is turf grass, Herbaceous
Plants, wood chips, mulch, or inorganic material;
(f) is located within 1.8 metres of the curb, unless it is turf grass, Herbaceous
Plants, wood chips, mulch, or inorganic material (any inorganic material, wood
chips, or mulch permitted under this subsection must be installed flush to the
curb).
(g) is located within 1.8 metres of the Roadway, where there is no curb, unless it
is turf grass, Herbaceous Plants, wood chips, mulch, or inorganic material (any
inorganic material, wood chips, or mulch permitted under this subsection must
be installed flush with the existing grade of the Boulevard and provide positive
drainage);
(h) is more than 20 centimeters in height, unless it is a Herbaceous Plant and
governed by subsection 2.1. of this by-law; or
(i) overflows onto the Sidewalk, Roadway or adjacent property;
(j) is located within 3m of the base/trunk of a Town Tree.
3.2. No Person shall permit turf grass to exceed a height as prescribed under Town by-
law No. 2006-23 (as amended), being a by-law respecting property standards on a
Boulevard abutting his or her property.
3.3. No Person shall alter an area of the Boulevard that is abutting his or her property
or regularly maintained by the Town or Region.
3.4 The Owner is to maintain their Driveway Apron in a state of good repair and control
material from the driveway from entering onto the Roadway. A road occupancy
permit is not required for repairs or replacement of a Driveway Apron, provided
there is no change to material, size or location.
3.5. The provisions of subsection 3.1 do not apply to snow.
3.6. The provisions of subsection 3.1 do not apply to anything on a Boulevard that is
permitted under Town by-Law No. 2010-073 (as amended), being a by-law to
establish and maintain a system for the collection, removal and disposal of
garbage, other refuse, yard waste materials, recyclable materials including blue
box materials and source separated organics in the Town.
3.7. Where an Owner has obtained written permission from the General Manager under
section 3.1, that Owner shall comply with any conditions set forth in the written
permission of the General Manager.
4. DAMAGE TO BOULEVARD
4.1. No Person shall damage, construct or re-construct a Sidewalk, curb, Driveway
Apron or Boulevard without the written permission of the General Manager.
4.2. For the purposes of Section 4.1, “Person” shall not include the Town, the
Region, a utility, or a contractor hired by the Town, Region or utility.
4.3. If a Boulevard, is damaged by the Town, the Region, a utility, or a contractor hired
by the Town, Region or utility, the person who that caused the damage shall only
be responsible for restoring (turf grass or asphalt for a Driveway Apron) that
Boulevard, and shall not be obligated to restore any alterations to the Boulevard
made by the Owner.
5. PENALTIES AND ENFORCEMENT
5.1. Where anything required to be done by an Owner in accordance with this by-law
is not done, the Town may do so and recover the cost of so doing by adding
the cost to the tax roll of the real property adjoining the Boulevard and collecting
the cost in the same manner and with the same priority as municipal taxes or in
the case of a contractor working on behalf of a utility company, the cost will be
added to the Road Occupancy Permit.
5.2. Every Person who contravenes a provision of this by-law is upon conviction guilty
of an offence and is liable to a fine recoverable under the Provincial Offences
Act, R.S.O., 1990, c. P. 33, as amended, or any successor legislation.
6. GENERAL
6.1. If any part, section, sub-section, clause or sub-clause of this by-law is for any
reason held to be invalid, such decision does not affect the validity of the remaining
portions of this by-law.
Short Title
6.2. This by-law may be cited as the "Boulevard By-Law."
Effective Date
This by-law shall come into force on November 15, 2016.
ENACTED AND PASSED this 15th day of November, 2016.

through the summer months.

original lease was executed in February 2025 for 16 months until April 2026.

Councillor Lewis
 Re: Use of the Public Parking Lot between Erie Road and Cambridge Road
Resolution:
Whereas the Crystal Beach Business Improvement Area Board of Management (CBBIA) has worked collaboratively with the Town of Fort Erie for more than nine years to develop and recommend parking management strategies for the Erie Road and Cambridge Road municipal parking lot, with the goal of ensuring the lot primarily serves customers and patrons of local businesses; and
Whereas the CBBIA has consistently recommended parking time limits and appropriate enforcement measures, particularly during the peak summer season, including a three-hour free parking model to support local businesses and encourage customer turnover; and
Whereas the Town of Fort Erie has invested in improvements to the parking lot and has implemented several parking management measures based on recommendations received from the CBBIA; and
Whereas Council recognizes the importance of continuing to work in partnership with the CBBIA and giving due consideration to its recommendations regarding parking management in the Crystal Beach business district; and
Whereas feedback received from the CBBIA, local businesses, and the community has identified concerns regarding the affordability of the proposed overnight parking pass fee;
Now therefore be it resolved,
That: Council direct staff to amend the proposed overnight parking pass fee for the Erie Road and Cambridge Road parking lot from $125 per month to $50 per month, consistent with feedback received from the CBBIA and community stakeholders; and be further directed to ensure proper signage is made to highlight business patrons and fee three hour parking for registered vehicles, and further
That: Council continue to work with the CBBIA and business community in the implementation and evaluation of parking management strategies to ensure the parking lot remains available and accessible for business patrons while supporting the economic vitality of the Crystal Beach commercial district.

File Number(s): ZBA-06-2026
The Planning, Building and By-law Services
Department received an application for a
Zoning By-law Amendment pursuant to Section
34 of the Planning Act, R.S.O. 1990, c. P.13.
The subject lands are designated Agricultural
and Environmental Protection in the Town’s
Official Plan. The subject lands are zoned
Agricultural (A) Zone, Environmental Protection
(EP) Zone, and Environmental Conservation
(EC) Overlay Zone in accordance with the
Town’s Comprehensive Zoning By-law 129-90,
as amended.
The purpose and effect of the proposed Zoning
By-law Amendment is to rezone the subject
lands from Agricultural (A) Zone to site-specific
Agricultural Zones to permit the conveyance of
a surplus farm dwelling as a result of farm consolidation. The proposed site-specific provisions
for the severed residential lot (Part 1) include reduced minimum lot area and minimum lot
frontage. The proposed site-specific provisions for the retained agricultural lot (Part 2) include
a reduced minimum interior side yard, and a provision that would prohibit any future residential
use of the subject lands in perpetuity. No changes are proposed to lands zoned Environmental
Protection (EP) Zone and Environmental Conservation (EC) Overlay Zone.
The subject lands are also subject to an application for Consent (File Number B26/25). This
Zoning By-law Amendment Application is being submitted as a condition of the Consent
Application.

Only the Minister, the applicant, specified persons, public bodies, and the registered owner of
the land to which the by-law would apply, as defined in the Planning Act, may appeal the
decision of Council to the Ontario Land Tribunal (OLT).
If a person or public body would otherwise have an ability to appeal the decision of Council to
the OLT, but the person or public body does not make oral submissions at a public meeting or
make written submissions to the Town of Fort Erie before the by-law is passed, the person or
public body is not entitled to appeal the decision.

submissions to the Town of Fort Erie before the by-law is passed, the person or public body
may not be added as a party to the hearing of an appeal before the OLT unless, in the opinion
of the OLT, there are reasonable grounds to do so.

6 Planning
a) Frontenac Islands Pre-Application By-law
Sonya Bolton, Manager of Community Planning, reviewed the need for the pre-
application process for planning matters so that applicants put forth the best application
possible. The reason for coming forward with this process now is due to the changes in
the Planning Act which came into force and effect this past year which affected the
timing for completion of planning reviews including refunds to the applicant if the
timelines are missed. North Frontenac has adopted this processes and Central
Frontenac will be considering it shortly.
Motion #: 74-23 Moved By: Deputy Mayor Saunders
Seconded By: Councillor Ackley
THAT the report regarding the new Pre-Application Consultation By-Law for planning
applications be received; and,
THAT the new Pre-Application Consultation By-Law included with this report as
Attachment 1 be approved by Council; and,
THAT the necessary by-law be presented to Council for all three readings.
Carried
b) B-02-23-W: Greenwood And Walters Application
S. Bolton advised that there are two public meetings this evening and outlined the
process to be used including notices and the requirement for anyone wishing to speak
to the application provide their full name, address and postal code. If a person does
Regular Meeting of Council Minutes
PJuangee 122 o, f2 10023 -4:00 PM
note provide oral or written submissions prior to Council's consideration of the
application, they may not entitled to appeal to the tribunal. She advised that the planner
will provide the background to the application, then the applicant, then Council and any
others wishing to speak to the applications.
Dmitry Kurylovich reviewed Application B-02-23, Greenwood/Walters. he noted the
zoning and official plan designations, noting that the severed parcel will be 0.4 hectares
and the retained parcel will 1.2 hectares. He noted the building envelopes on the
proposed land as well as a proposed septic systems layout. Mr. Kurylovich noted that it
does comply with Building Code requirements.
He overviewed the comments received to date including the CRCA and the Township of
South Frontenac regarding septic suitability. Mr. Kurylovich stated that the County had
not received any comments from the public.
Deputy Mayor Saunders asked if the development agreement would restrict further
building such as a boat house. D. Kurylovich noted that the restrictions are to ensure
that the septic system area is guaranteed, leaving the applicant/owner with the
opportunity to apply for other structures.
Mayor Greenwood-Speers asked for confirmation on the entrance to the severed lot
including direct access to Road 96. This was confirmed.
The Mayor asked if there were any present or on Zoom who would like to speak to the
application. The agent for the property owner stated they agreed with the
recommendations.
Motion #: 75-23 Moved By: Deputy Mayor Saunders
Seconded By: Councillor Ackley
THAT consent application Number B-02-23-W, for the property located at Part lot 17,
18, and 9 on Wolfe Island Old Survey; Parts 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12 to 15, and 17 on
Registered Plan 13R14048, municipal address 510 Road 96 for the severance of a new
waterfront lot and a right-of-way easement along the retained lands for dock access, be
approved, subject to the conditions noted in Appendix A of the Planning Report;
THAT the Clerk shall issue the Notice of Decision in accordance with the requirements
of the Planning Act, including providing the Notice of Decision to the applicant, any
person or public body that made a written request to be notified, and any other person
or public body prescribed; and,
THAT all conditions outlined in the Notice of Decision shall be completed, and the
Certificate of Official issued, within a period of two years after the Notice of Decision
was issued, as required by the Planning Act.
Carried
c) B-10-23-W Caldwell Application
Regular Meeting of Council Minutes
PJuangee 132 o, f2 10023 -4:00 PM
D. Kurylovich provided a description of the proposed lot addition adding that it will also
address the encroachment of a garage on neighbouring property. The severance will
be approximately 7 hectares with waterfrontage on the St. Lawrence River/Lake
Ontario. The retained lands will be 18.6 hectares. He outlined the zoning and official
plan designations. The application is large enough that septic review and review by the
CRCA was not needed as there is sufficient room to build.
Council did not have any questions. The public were asked, through Zoom if they had
any question, none responded. The applicant was not present.
Motion #: 76-23 Moved By: Councillor Jablonicky
Seconded By: Councillor Hulton
THAT consent application Number B-10-23-W (Caldwell), for the property located at

addition parcel for the purpose of enlarging 73 South Shore Road, be approved, subject
to the conditions noted in Appendix A of the Planning Report;
THAT the Clerk shall issue the Notice of Decision in accordance with the requirements
of the Planning Act, including providing the Notice of Decision to the applicant, any
person or public body that made a written request to be notified, and any other person
or public body prescribed; and,
THAT all conditions outlined in the Notice of Decision shall be completed, and the
Certificate of Official issued, within a period of two years after the Notice of Decision
was issued, as required by the Planning Act.
Carried

Agendas, Minutes and Meetings
Live meetings
Town of Georgina Council meetings are available in person in the Council chambers as well as online. This hybrid model allows staff members, Council members and the public to participate in person or virtually. All committee and board meetings are being held virtually at this time.
View the meetings
Council meetings are broadcast through the Town’s live streaming tool. Anyone interested in speaking during the public portion of the meeting may attend in person or virtually. To participate virtually, pre-registration is required. To pre-register for a meeting, a Request to Speak Form must be submitted to the Clerks Division by noon the day before the meeting. To learn more about attending or participating in a Council meeting, and to find the Request to Speak form, visit georgina.ca/CouncilMeetings.
How to watch
To stream a live meeting, select the appropriate meeting date above at the time of the meeting. Approximately half an hour prior to the start of the meeting, a link will appear (alongside the agenda) to livestream the meeting. Start viewing the meeting by selecting the link displayed. 
All Council meetings are available to view on community television or online from Rogers TV.(link is external)

2026 meeting schedule
Agendas, meeting minutes and broadcast archives
Agendas are normally available online on the Thursday preceding the posted meeting date. Meeting minutes are the official record of all meetings and are available for download once they have been approved by Council and have been released by the Clerk’s Division for online posting. The live broadcasts are archived upon meeting completion and can be viewed at a later time.
Looking for Council agendas and minutes from past meetings?
If you are looking for the Council agendas and minutes prior to 2021, visit the Georgina Electronic-records Management System (GEMS) for a full listing.
Having trouble searching for the document you need? Please see this informative article on how to search using FileHold. (link is external)

Council Meetings
Town of Georgina Council meets throughout the year to make decisions on municipal matters, from passing bylaws to adopting committee recommendations.
Council meetings are open to public and held at the Civic Centre in the Council Chambers. The meetings are a hybrid model, providing staff, Council members and the public the option of participating either in person or virtually. In addition, Council meetings are live streamed  on the Town of Georgina Agendas, Minutes and Meetings page. Should you be unable to attend the meetings, you are welcome to listen through the Live/Archived Broadcasts webpage.
Council Meetings
Hybrid Council meetings 
Council meetings are in-person hybrid model at the Replacement Civic Centre. 
To view or listen to meetings only, access the relevant live stream on the Agendas, Minutes and Meetings page. Members of the public can watch live during the time of the meeting or view a recording later.
To participate in a Council meeting, the appropriate form must be submitted to the Clerks’ Division within the prescribed timeframe. Learn more in the “Speak at Council or committee meetings” section below.
Contact clerks@georgina.ca(link sends email) with any questions regarding attending or participating in Council meetings.
Speak at Council or committee meetings
Public consultation is an important part of the Council and committee process. If you wish to speak at Council or committee meetings – either in-person or virtually - you must first complete one of the following forms:
Delegation Request Form – Complete this form if you wish to speak or make a presentation regarding an item that is not listed on a Council agenda. Delegations are limited to five minutes. A five-minute extension to speak may be decided by a majority vote of Council. Regardless of participation method, Delegation Request Forms must be received no later than 10 a.m. on the Monday 10 days prior to the Wednesday meeting to pre-register.
Request to Speak Form - Complete this form to request to speak at a Council meeting on an agenda item. Speakers may speak once for up to five minutes. Virtual requests to speak must be submitted by noon the day before the meeting. In‑person requests to speak are encouraged to be submitted in advance and may also be submitted prior to the start of the meeting.
Committee of Adjustment Request to Speak Form
Be advised, the name and address of anyone submitting comments will appear in the public record and will be posted online following the meeting.

Town of Gore Bay
Strategic Plan
INTRODUCTION
The Town of Gore Bay, located on the North Channel of Lake Huron, is nestled
between two splendid, tree covered bluffs. Incorporated in 1890, Gore Bay is one
of the larger communities on Manitoulin with a permanent population of just over
900. Gore Bay is the judicial centre of Manitoulin, and one of the island's
commercial and professional centres.
The town features one of the largest marinas on Manitoulin Island. During the
summer months the population and activity of the town flourishes as boaters and
tourists from around Ontario and the Great Lakes regions flock to the area. The
area is popular with cottagers and vacationers during the summer months. Gore
Bay is an attractive town where there is lots to see and do
This strategic plan captures Council’s key priorities, but it does not include the
multitude of responsibilities to it citizens or businesses. The plan focuses on the
direction Council wants to make based on all the community input received during
the planning process.
This plan outlines the key areas that Town Council believes are fundamentally
important for the community’s sustainability, economic competitiveness, and
quality of life.
Town of Gore Bay
Strategic Plan
1. EXECUTIVE REPORT
The Town of Gore Bay began the process of developing its 2022-2027 Strategic
Plan during an unprecedented time in history. It is imperative to gather information
from various groups within the community including residents, business owners,
and the many visitors to our community. The Covid-19 Pandemic provided
difficulties in establishing an open dialogue between the public body and Town
Council.
While challenging at times the process allowed for a review of how business is
done, asking questions about what can be done differently and resulting in creative
solutions to opportunities that were presented.
A question asked by many is what is the point of a strategic plan?
• The process of writing the plan provides clarity for Council towards
accomplishing goals
• If capital is required from outside sources investors want to see a plan that
demonstrates a solid understanding of a vision for the community.
• The plan prioritizes what tasks are important
• With growth and change the plan offers a common understanding of the vision
for the future
A common theme that was reoccurring was a want and need for increased
communication and a desire for a strong and vibrant community. Constituents want
more opportunities to be engaged with Town Council.
Town of Gore Bay
Strategic Plan
Success comes from a united approach from a community working together to
achieve common goals.
Through the gathering of input from the community via surveys, stakeholders
sessions, and the strategic planning committee group, the plan sets a clear vision
for projects that are important to the community.
The plan will be reviewed yearly, and a report will be published and made available
for public review.

Town of Gore Bay
Strategic Plan
2. MAYOR’S REPORT
On behalf of Council and our staff, I am looking forward to the next 4 years
as we present the Strategic Plan that guides the direction of our
community. We are at an exciting time in the development of our
community as we continue to grow and prosper as a known destination on
Manitoulin.
This Plan has been developed with input from the public, community
groups, business, staff and Council in a variety of formats. As a result, the
Strategic Plan reflects the values, vision, and priorities of our
community. This Plan recognizes our role as a community-builder and our
commitment to delivering municipal programs and services that meet the
needs of the public today and into the future. We have set out ambitious
goals. Next, we’ll develop action plans to achieve those goals and monitor
and report on our achievements. As always, Council will be looking to
achieve these goals while balancing affordability and excellent service.

A starting point for any strategic planning is to perform a situational analysis which
refers to an evaluation of both external and internal environmental factors. A
SWOT exercise was performed which includes brainstorming all strengths,
weaknesses, opportunities, and threats. This is a useful tool to evaluate the current
conditions of an organization and set a position for reference for the future.

A Strategic Plan should identify a preferred outlook for a community. Ask the
questions what do you want to achieve? What kind of community do you want to
live in?
Performing a visioning exercise at the beginning of the strategic process helps act
as guide for the rest by building a foundation for the remaining areas to follow.
The Town of Gore Bay’s Vision Statement focusses on the people in the
community and a quality of life to achieve. This statement will be used as a
sounding board for every action and decision made by Gore Bay Council.

6. MANAGEMENT
Implementation will involve aligning resources, activities and opportunities with
the vision developed through the strategic planning process. Key performance
metrics will be used to evaluate if Council decisions are in alignment with the
strategic plan.
Questions that will be asked include:
• Did we achieve what we set out to do?
• Did actions taken have a desired outcome?
• Are we any closer to achieving our goals?
Metrics used will be tangible and measurable but can and will be in the form of
progress reports. Outside influences contribute to successes or failures in
achieving goals. Metrics will also only include an evaluation of components that
the Town has exclusive accountability for.
Gore Bay Council will continue to seek input from its constituent body.
The strategic plan is an evergreen document, meaning that it will be adapted as
evaluations are made.
Yearly evaluations of the 2022-2027 Strategic Plan will be communicated to the
public by a report.
A Mayor’s Report will be provided to the Public yearly to provide an update on all
Town projects.

Public Meeting Proposed Zoning By-Law Amendment - 50 Emma Street South Z01-2025, 2025-022
This item has Video
 Mayor Soloman requested the Manager of Planning to provide a summary of the proposed Zoning By-Law Amendment.
Mark Kluge, Manager of Planning, advised the purpose of the public meeting is to obtain public comments and feedback regarding a new proposed zoning amendment application relating to the property located at 50 Emma Street South, which comprises of the municipal addresses 40, 50 and 60 Emma Street South.  Mr. Kluge advised that this is a new application proposing a 5-storey, 24-unit residential building, whereas the previous application proposed a 4-storey, 18 unit structure, with 38 parking spaces and that the 4-storey application remains open.
Mr. Kluge advised that during the public meeting for the proposed 4-storey, 18- unit residential building, with 38 parking spaces, Council's comments included interest in increasing height and density. The applicant has considered Council's comments and made a decision to revisit the building's design and have prepared a new application which proposes a 5-storey residential building with 24 residential units and 38 parking spaces.  Mr. Kluge advised a County Official Plan amendment was required for the previous application.  Dufferin County Council has approved the Official Plan Amendment, OPA 7, with permitted use being Urban Residential. He stated the new application will require site specific zoning to a Multiple Residential Zone to permit a multi-unit residential building and zoning exceptions for maximum building height, density and off-street parking. He advised site plan and condominium applications are also required but are not part of the public process. This application will require 12 servicing allocations. He stated technical comments have been received and shared with the applicant for their review. Engineering comments have not been received, but will be reviewed by the Town upon receipt and included in a future report to Council. Mr. Kluge advised one letter with public comments has been received.  This letter has been shared with Council and the applicant. Mr. Kluge stated the deadline for receipt of public comments is March 21, 2025 and all comments received will be addressed in a future report to Council. He advised no decision on the proposed application would be made at this meeting. 
Mayor Soloman thanked Mr. Kluge and requested Council provide their questions and comments.  
Councillor Latam sought clarification regarding increased density and reduction of parking. Mr. Kluge provided clarification, stating that the proposed density is 75 units per hectare, whereas 50 units per hectare is required.  Additionally, 2 parking spaces per unit are required under our zoning by-law, and the applicant is requesting a reduction to 1.58 spaces per unit.
Councillor Jonker inquired as to number of bedrooms per unit. 
Andrew Wildeboer and William Wildeboer, owners of the lands, and representatives of Sheldon Creek Developments Inc., appeared at the meeting to provide comments and answered questions regarding the proposed application.  
Andrew Wildeboer advised the building will consist of 20 two-bedroom units and 4 one-bedroom units. 
Councillor Jonker inquired as to whether public comments received would be addressed. The Manager of Planning advised public comments would addressed in a future Council report. 
Councillor Jonker expressed concerns regarding the appropriateness of a 5-storey residential building in this location and inquired of the applicants as to the motivation for a 5-storey residential building. 
Andrew Wildeboer advised motivation included economics, the housing crisis and to address comments received from Council for increased density.
Mayor Soloman inquired as to whether a fire ladder truck was required for this application. Mr. Kluge advised a fire ladder truck is not a specific requirement for this application.
Deputy Mayor Rentsch stated he is not in support of the proposed increase in density or reductions in parking and request the applicants complete a Shade Study.  His comments included that direction was not provided by Council to the applicants to increase density and stated these were comments from a certain Member of Council. 
Mr. Kluge advised that the applicants have kept the 4-storey application open.    
Councillor Dart stated he is not in support of the proposed 5-storey residential building in this location.  His comments included the Town can get by with what we have for fire services.  He stated he was not in support of reduced parking and expressed concerns regarding the slope to the neighbouring properties, commenting that upper units would look into current Taylor Drive residences. 
Councillor Latam inquired as the affordability of units. 
William Wildeboer stated the proposed 5-storey residential building provides additional availability. The additional storey maximizes unit availability and by increasing the building foot print it assists with affordability.
Councillor Dart inquired as to price range for the units. 
William Wildeboer stated one bedroom units would potentially be listed in the range of low $500,000, with 2 bedroom units listed in low $600,000. 
Andrew Wildeboer stated a large part of the price is the underground parking. 
Councillor Latam requested engineering comments include clarification on whether lay-buys in front of Emma Street will be installed as the site plan provided is unclear. Mr. Kluge advised clarification would be sought from the Town's engineers. 
Council Latam inquired as to whether the number of stories would affect the units' prices. 
Andrew Wildeboer stated they would need to conduct a re-evaluation if the number of stories was decreased and stated comparable units in Orangeville are listed for an additional $150,000. 
Mayor Soloman thanked Council for providing their comments. 
Mark Kluge advised public commenting would remain open until March 21, 2025. 
Resolution:2025-02-34

Seconded by:P. Rentsch

CARRIED

Proposal:
The purpose and effect of the proposed Official Plan Amendment is to establish a site-specific policy area to
permit the creation of a residential lot in the ‘Agricultural Reserve’ designation.
The purpose and effect of the proposed Zoning By-law Amendment is to change the zoning classification on
the lands to be severed from the ‘A’, Agricultural Zone, to the ‘A(S)’, Agricultural Special Zone in order to limit
the use to residential, and to change the zoning classification on the lands to be retained from the ‘A’,
Agricultural Zone, to the ‘A(S)’, Agricultural Special Zone to prohibit residential uses.
The subject lands are designated ‘Agriculture Reserve’ within the City of Greater Sudbury Official Plan, are
zoned ‘A’, Agricultural within the City of Greater Sudbury Zoning By-law, and are regulated by Conservation
Sudbury (NDCA). The subject lands contain regulated features of Conservation Sudbury including erosion and
flood hazards associated with a tributary of the Whitson River.
The lands proposed to be severed would have a lot area of 0.4 ha and a frontage of 61.5 m along Montee
Rouleau. The lands contain a single detached dwelling with an attached deck, two accessory buildings, and a
pool. The lands are serviced by a private septic system and a municipal water connection and are accessed
from Montee Rouleau.
The lands to be retained would have an area of 30.7 ha and a frontage of 171 m along Seguin Street. The
lands contain a barn and a shed, are unserviced, and are accessed from Seguin Street.
Surrounding uses are agricultural and rural in nature.

4.3.3 Lot Creation and Lot Adjustments
1. Lot creation in prime agricultural areas is discouraged and may only be permitted in accordance with
provincial guidance for:
a) agricultural uses, provided that the lots are of a size appropriate for the type of agricultural use(s)
common in the area and are sufficiently large to maintain flexibility for future changes in the type or
size of agricultural operations;
b) agriculture-related uses, provided that any new lot will be limited to a minimum size needed to
accommodate the use and appropriate sewage and water services;
c) one new residential lot per farm consolidation for a residence surplus to an agricultural operation,
provided that:
1. the new lot will be limited to a minimum size needed to accommodate the use and appropriate
sewage and water services; and

Dates for Council and Committees meetings along with the agenda and minutes are available on the Meeting Calendar on our Council Portal. The Minutes and Agendas for all Committee meetings are also available in Document Center. 
Agendas are published to the public 3 days before the scheduled meeting date.
Council Meetings are generally held the first and third Wednesday of every month at 10:00 am in the Council Chambers located at 206 Toronto Street South Markdale, ON and available for zoom attendance in a hybrid format.  
Council and Committee of the Whole meetings are offered in a hybrid format, with all other Committees being held either virtually or in person only (no hybrid format available). 
There are several options when wishing to appear before Council. Please see the Procedural By-law, as amended for the rules governing the proceedings of all meetings of the Municipality and Policy A09-C11 for Electronic Participation. 
Communications addressed to Council
Communications sent to the Clerk's Office addressed to all of Council is either forwarded to Council via email, placed on a Council agenda, or included in the Council Information Package. Any member of Council may pull any item from the weekly Council Information Package to be placed on an upcoming agenda. Weekly Council Information Packages are available for public viewing here. Council Information Packages are generally available for viewing for a minimum of 1 year if not added to an agenda by a member of Council. *Please note that this does not include email communications where Council has also been cc'd as it is deemed that they are already in receipt of such information. 
If you wish to email all of Council, please email council@greyhighlands.ca. 
To contact the Clerk's department, please email clerks@greyhighlands.ca.
